title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 129
paragraphs: Then, when the day appointed for the wedding feast had come, and for Cleisthenes himself to declare which of the suitors he was choosing, Cleisthenes sacrificed a hundred oxen and feasted both the suitors and all the people of Sicyon. When the meal was finished, the suitors began to compete with one another in music and in speeches for the company's entertainment; and as the drinking went on and Hippocleides was commanding great attention, he told the flute-player to strike up a dance tune. The flute-player did so, and Hippocleides danced. He pleased himself with his own dancing, but Cleisthenes was beginning to look on the whole thing with suspicion. After a while Hippocleides called for a table to be brought in, and when it came, he first danced Laconian figures on top of it, then Attic ones, and then, thirdly, he planted his head on the table and kicked his legs in the air. Cleisthenes, during the first and second performances, though he was already revolted at the thought of having Hippocleides for a son-in-law because of his dancing and shamelessness, restrained himself, not wanting to burst out at him in anger. But when he saw him waving his legs around in the air, he could hold back no longer and said: “Son of Tisander, you have danced your marriage away!” And Hippocleides answered: “Hippocleides doesn't care!”
